clinicalPearls: CMV is a beta-herpesvirus carried for life after infection; the infection is usually silent, and reactivation syndromes emerge predominantly when T-lymphocyte-mediated immunity is compromised (organ transplantation, lymphoid neoplasms, HIV, or critical illness in the ICU) (p.1512).

In immunocompetent hosts beyond the neonatal period, the most common manifestation is a heterophile-antibody-negative mononucleosis syndrome; unlike EBV mononucleosis, exudative pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy are rare, though splenomegaly, prolonged high fever, fatigue and malaise are common (p.1513-1514).
The characteristic laboratory finding in CMV mononucleosis is relative lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes (predominantly activated CD8+ T cells); heterophile antibodies are absent (p.1514).

Congenital CMV is the commonest congenital infection; most congenital infections are clinically inapparent at birth, yet 7-11% of asymptomatically infected infants develop sensorineural hearing loss over 5 years (p.1512-1513).

Clinical disease in the fetus/newborn is related largely to PRIMARY maternal infection rather than reactivation; primary first-trimester infection carries up to 40-50% risk of sensorineural complications (p.1513).

Preferred diagnosis is detection of virus/antigen/DNA, most commonly quantitative nucleic acid testing (QNAT) by PCR; the pp65 antigenemia immunofluorescence assay is an alternative, and CMV DNA in CSF aids diagnosis of CMV encephalitis or polyradiculopathy (p.1515).

In persons with HIV, end-organ CMV disease (especially retinitis) occurs particularly when CD4+ counts fall below 50/uL; flares of CMV retinitis can occur shortly after starting antiretroviral therapy as an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) (p.1514).

An immune-complex glomerulopathy has been observed in some CMV-infected patients after renal transplantation, and CMV mononucleosis can produce transient autoantibodies (cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factors, cold agglutinins, antinuclear antibodies) via polyclonal B-cell activation (p.1512-1514).
Pathology shows enlarged 'cytomegalic' cells (2-4x normal) with an eccentric intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo producing the classic 'owl's eye' appearance (p.1513).
harrison.pathophysiology: CMV is a beta-herpesvirus with double-stranded DNA, icosahedral symmetry and a lipoprotein envelope; it replicates in the cell nucleus and can establish either lytic/productive or latent infection. After primary infection the virus persists indefinitely in multiple cell types and organs (silent latency). Primary infection in late childhood/adulthood elicits a vigorous CD8+ T-lymphocyte response producing atypical lymphocytes and a mononucleosis-like illness, with polyclonal B-cell activation generating autoantibodies. When host T-cell responses are compromised by disease or iatrogenic immunosuppression, latent virus reactivates; chronic antigenic stimulation under immunosuppression (e.g., post-transplant) is an ideal setting for CMV disease, and potent T-cell suppressants (antithymocyte globulin, alemtuzumab) markedly raise CMV syndrome rates. CMV itself further depresses T-lymphocyte responsiveness, predisposing to superinfection by other opportunists. Congenital disease arises chiefly from primary maternal infection; transmission to transplant/transfusion recipients reflects silent infection in donor tissues (p.1512-1513).
additionalDifferentials: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infectious mononucleosis (heterophile-positive, with prominent exudative pharyngitis and cervical adenopathy) versus CMV mononucleosis (heterophile-negative)
Congenital cytomegalic inclusion disease must be distinguished from congenital syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rubella, Zika, herpes simplex virus, and bacterial sepsis (p.1513)
CMV pneumonitis differential includes Pneumocystis, other viral/bacterial/fungal pneumonias, pulmonary hemorrhage, and irradiation or cytotoxic drug injury (p.1514)
CMV retinopathy must be distinguished from toxoplasmosis, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus retinitis (p.1514)
infectionMimics: Congenital rubella, Zika, herpes simplex virus, and syphilis (in neonates)
Herpes simplex virus and Candida retinitis/esophagitis
nonInfectiousMimics: Pulmonary hemorrhage and radiation- or cytotoxic-drug-induced lung injury (mimicking CMV pneumonitis)
Allograft rejection (overlapping with CMV syndrome in transplant recipients)
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative nucleic acid testing (QNAT) for CMV DNA by PCR in blood or other specimens (preferred; same assay should be used for serial comparison)
CMV pp65 antigenemia immunofluorescence assay on peripheral-blood leukocytes
CMV DNA PCR in cerebrospinal fluid for suspected encephalitis or polyradiculopathy
Viral culture on human fibroblast monolayers, including the rapid overnight shell vial assay with monoclonal antibody to immediate-early antigen

Serology: CMV IgG (may take up to 4 weeks to rise after primary infection) and CMV IgM (false positives possible with rheumatoid factor); serology mainly stratifies transplant risk and is NOT recommended to diagnose acute disease in immunocompromised patients
Histopathology/biopsy demonstrating 'owl's eye' cytomegalic inclusions for tissue-invasive disease
redFlags: Retinitis in an immunocompromised host (especially HIV with CD4+ <50/uL) - threat to vision
Colitis or gastrointestinal ulceration with risk of bleeding or perforation
Pneumonitis (tachypnea, hypoxemia, nonproductive cough with bilateral interstitial/reticulonodular infiltrates)
Persistent viremia with multi-organ involvement, pancytopenia and hypotension (associated with fatal disease)
Symptomatic congenital infection (petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly with cerebral calcifications, intrauterine growth retardation)
harrison.prognosis: Immunocompetent CMV mononucleosis is almost always self-limited (illness lasting 2-6 weeks); most patients recover without sequelae, though postviral asthenia may persist for months and fatal infection is rare. Severely affected congenitally infected infants have a poor prognosis with a mortality of about 5% and few survivors escaping intellectual or hearing impairment; 7-11% of asymptomatically infected neonates still develop sensorineural hearing loss over 5 years. In immunocompromised hosts, untreated CMV may progress to severe end-organ disease; CMV disease is an independent risk factor for both graft loss and death after organ transplantation, and high blood viral loads in HIV predict severe disease and death (p.1513-1514).
pitfalls: Tissue-invasive CMV disease (e.g., gastrointestinal) may be present despite NEGATIVE blood CMV antigenemia and viral-load testing - diagnosis may require endoscopic biopsy with histopathology, not blood viremia alone (p.1514).

Isolation of CMV from urine, stool, or saliva does NOT by itself prove acute infection, since excretion may persist for months to years; detection of viremia by QNAT or antigenemia is a better predictor (p.1515).
Serology is NOT recommended to diagnose acute disease in immunocompromised patients; IgG may not rise for up to 4 weeks and rheumatoid factor can cause false-positive IgM (p.1515).
CMV detection in blood does not equate to end-organ disease; clinical and tissue correlation is required.
Universal ganciclovir/valganciclovir prophylaxis is bone-marrow suppressive, favoring preemptive strategies in HSCT recipients (p.1515).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison frames CMV by host and syndrome rather than a formal grading scale: (1) congenital CMV - subclinical to severe disseminated cytomegalic inclusion disease; (2) perinatal CMV - usually asymptomatic; (3) immunocompetent CMV mononucleosis - heterophile-negative, self-limited; (4) CMV in the immunocompromised host - asymptomatic infection/viremia, 'CMV syndrome' (febrile leukopenia), and tissue-invasive end-organ disease (pneumonitis, colitis/GI disease, hepatitis, esophagitis, retinitis, encephalitis/polyradiculopathy), stratified by population in Table 200-1 (fetus/neonate, organ transplant recipient, HSCT recipient, person with HIV) (p.1513).
